description: Common Ground talks from BSides Las Vegas 2025.

talks.title: Rewriting the Playbook: Smarter Vulnerability Management with EPSSv3, CVSSv4, SSVC & VEX Frameworks
talks.teaser: Explains how EPSS, CVSSv4, SSVC and VEX can be combined to cut vulnerability triage noise.
talks.summary:
The talk, given by Avinash Nutalapati, starts from the limits of relying on CVSS version 3 scores alone. A severity number says little about reachability in a given environment, exploits often appear long after disclosure, and attackers chain weaknesses rather than using one bug. CVSS version 4 adds attack requirements, user interaction and downstream impact.

The middle section covers three complementary frameworks. EPSS, a model from FIRST, estimates the chance of exploitation within 30 days and is refreshed daily, so it sets the order of work, though low scores should not be dismissed outright. VEX records whether a vendor component is actually affected, with outcomes such as not affected, fixed and under investigation. SSVC, developed at Carnegie Mellon and adapted by CISA, is a decision tree ending in track, attend or act, and should be customized for sectors such as finance or healthcare.

The closing part proposes a phased rollout: EPSS and KEV data first, then SBOM pilots, CVSS 4 and VEX work, and SSVC last, with automation of tagging and ticket creation throughout. Practitioners need skilled staff and suitable tooling, and should ask vendors for SBOMs, since a clean internal result does not mean a supplier is unaffected.

talks.title: The Not So Boring Threat Model of CSP-Managed NHI's
talks.teaser: Compares provider-managed non-human identities across AWS, Google Cloud and Microsoft, and where each one is vulnerable.
talks.summary:
Kat Traxler walks through the identities that cloud providers create and operate on a customer's behalf, including AWS service-linked roles, Google Cloud service agents and Microsoft first-party app service principals. These are not the users or roles an administrator builds, which makes them easy to overlook. The talk uses a threat-modeling approach: what is being built, what can go wrong, and what can be done about it.

Risks differ by provider. AWS's multi-tenant design lets one provider principal act across many customer accounts, so a bucket policy that trusts it broadly can be abused in a cross-service confused deputy scenario. Google's service agents are single-tenant per project but often start with powerful permissions, so a user who cannot read a bucket directly may reach it through the agent. For Microsoft, a long-term credential can be added to a first-party service principal, letting an attacker authenticate as that service, a capability the speaker said AWS and Google Cloud do not offer.

Controls differ too. Only AWS lets a customer restrict these trusted principals directly, using condition keys in resource policies. On Google Cloud, the fix lies with the provider, so issues should be reported to Google. On Microsoft, an app instance property lock could block credential additions, but only the publisher can set it and it has not been applied consistently. The speaker suggested detective monitoring as the main lever for customers and closed with an informal grading of the three designs.

talks.title: The Unbearable Weight of Commercial Licensing. Combining Closed Systems with Open Source Defense
talks.teaser: Weighs commercial security tools against open-source threat intelligence, with a walkthrough of the MISP sharing platform.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a brief history of the internet, pointing out that much of its foundation came from open-source work such as the Linux kernel, git and the RFC process. The speaker, an analyst with about ten years in information security, then argues that commercial security products bring their own problems: licensing tiers that grow hard to navigate, data retention windows that make older activity difficult to revisit, and alerts that arrive with little explanation.

The middle of the talk turns to MISP, an open-source threat intelligence sharing platform. It began in 2011 as a way to stop analysts from repeating the same malware research, and it is now community-driven, with European public bodies involved and around 6,000 organizations running instances that can be found online. The speaker covered the event and attribute model, the IDS flag that marks indicators for blocking, correlation across events, taxonomies and galaxies mapped to MITRE ATT&CK, feed caching, role-based permissions, audit logging, and automation through APIs and webhooks. A live demo on a self-hosted instance showed how indicators tied to one user were linked to earlier incidents.

The closing questions covered server maintenance and trust. The speaker described auditing a default install and fixing a world-readable configuration file, and stressed that organizations should trust each other before indicators are pushed automatically to blocking devices. The practical takeaway is that an open platform can keep shareable context beyond a vendor's retention window, provided the sharing relationships are vetted first.

talks.title: Agentic AI Malware: Why the Cybersecurity Battle Isn’t Over
talks.teaser: Assesses whether agentic AI malware is already a real threat, with a PowerShell proof of concept and defender takeaways.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a puzzle: headlines describe AI malware that adapts to any defense, yet sample volumes and telemetry show few confirmed cases. The speaker separates malware that was merely written with an LLM from malware that calls a model while it runs. Examples include scripts with leftover AI-style comments, jailbroken or uncensored models, and a recent campaign that used a hosted code model to generate reconnaissance commands during intrusions.

The middle section presents a proof-of-concept PowerShell loader that carries no fixed payload. Each run it asks a hosted model for a command, executes it, feeds errors back, and stores the working prompt in the registry. The speaker then adds an orchestrator, research agents and tool agents that communicate locally. In testing against several commercial EDR products, the evasion attempts were ultimately detected, and the demo showed how repeated, varied attempts leave noticeable patterns.

The conclusion is that AI mainly speeds up planning, orchestration and exploitation at scale, and makes evasion more dynamic, but it does not yet give attackers a decisive edge. Basic defenses still work: behavior-based detection, file reputation, and monitoring of traffic to LLM services. Practitioners should expect an AI-versus-AI contest rather than a collapse of existing controls.

talks.title: Keeping Our History Alive: The Hacker’s Guide to Sticker Preservation
talks.teaser: Shows how to peel, clean, and reapply laptop stickers without ruining them or losing what they signal.
talks.summary:
Brian Baskin opens by framing laptop stickers as a way for people in hacker communities to show their interests, affiliations and history. In a crowd of thousands at a conference, a sticker can reveal a shared skill set, a favourite tool, an old CTF, or a past event, and it can signal who is worth talking to. He also touches on how stickers mark cultural moments, from old groups and conference branding to in-jokes that only a small circle recognises.

The middle of the talk turns to the practical problem of losing these stickers when people upgrade hardware. Baskin explains that a sticker is made of layers, including vinyl, printed ink, laminate and adhesive, and that a simple pry with a razor often lifts the laminate instead of the glue, leaving residue behind. He compared solvents, including acetone, isopropyl alcohol and heptane-based removers. Acetone cleaned well but discoloured printing, while the heptane products gathered the adhesive into a gel that could be scraped off. He also tested heat from a hair dryer, a heat gun and steam. Too much heat damaged the laptop screen, and steam warped the vinyl.

To finish, he covers reapplication. Options include a specific spray adhesive, double-sided transfer tape, or scanning a sticker and recutting it with a vinyl cutter. His main recommendation is to move stickers onto a clamshell case or a silicone laptop skin, so they can be removed, reused and carried over to future hardware without risking the device itself.

talks.title: Risk it for the Biscuit: Crunching the Numbers on Cyber Threats
talks.teaser: Shows how to rank security risks by business impact and threat context rather than by headlines or CVSS scores.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that many organizations measure cyber risk poorly, chasing headlines, zero-day news or CVSS scores instead of the causes that actually drive incidents. The speaker points to human-driven mistakes as the most common root of breaches and cites recent high-profile intrusions where a missing second factor or a weak account-recovery process made the difference.

The middle section covers the building blocks of a risk program: a complete asset inventory, layered data flow diagrams with labelled trust boundaries, and threat models built by repeatedly asking what is being built, what can go wrong and how it is handled. The speaker separates vulnerabilities from risks, since a risk exists only when a threat meets a weakness, and urges impact to be described in business terms such as lost revenue rather than offline servers. Mitigations go into a risk tracker with owner, impact, mitigation and review date, and accepted risk should be signed off by an executive with authority to own it.

The closing message is to stay focused on the most likely and most impactful risks instead of reacting to every new zero-day, because chasing the latest issue can leave larger gaps open. In the Q&A, the advice for requirements that teams keep deprioritizing was to escalate through executive levels and bring in legal teams, who can frame obligations in terms leadership understands.

talks.title: Thwarting Key Extraction and Supply Chain attacks by Detonating GPUs
talks.teaser: Shows how physically destroying GPUs with detonators can deny attackers key extraction and chip reuse.
talks.summary:
The talk asks why a device owner might want a built-in self-destruct for GPUs and other accelerators, since whoever physically holds the hardware is not always a party you trust. The concerns covered include key extraction through physical side channels, tampering along the supply chain, and deploying expensive hardware in regions where political relationships may change. The goal is to destroy the chip fast enough to deny access, and to do it at data center scale.

The speaker walked through the options tested. Nanothermite deposited on a chip was difficult to ignite, especially with a heat sink attached, and it left the chip largely intact, so it was ruled out. Small detonators placed inside the heat sink, using the copper cold plate as the striking surface, produced complete destruction of the GPU die, while the memory stacks were less thoroughly destroyed. Detonators were also aged at elevated temperature to check they would stay stable over a long service life. Layers of metal foam, carbon fiber and a Kevlar sleeve were used to contain the blast on both SXM and PCIe form factors.

To close, the speaker outlined next steps: cleaner packaging, regulatory exemptions for handling and shipping, and integration with tamper detection or an emergency scram trigger. For practitioners, the takeaway is that any destruction design has to balance effectiveness, cost, containment and legal limits, not just speed.

talks.title: So… You want to build your own hacking device…
talks.teaser: Walks through choosing boards, languages and parts for building your own small Wi-Fi and IoT gadgets.
talks.summary:
This introductory talk is aimed at people who want to build their own small hacking and IoT gadgets. The speaker, a penetration tester, explains why building your own hardware can be cheaper and more flexible than buying commercial tools such as the Flipper Zero, which is costly to lose on a drone. He compares microcontroller boards, including the ESP32, Raspberry Pi Pico and Arduino Nano, on wireless support, voltage requirements and memory, and then contrasts MicroPython with Arduino C for programming them.

Next he covers prototyping approaches, moving from breadboards for quick tests to perforated boards and custom-fabricated boards for devices that need to be mobile or sold. He recommends starter kits with good documentation, and advises checking whether a part has MicroPython examples and whether it has reached end of life. Two example projects follow. The first is a portable connectivity monitor that uses an LED and a small screen to show whether the internet is up. The second is a Wi-Fi captive-portal device that imitates a network login page to collect submitted passwords, with a design built around remote retrieval and limited visibility.

The talk closes with ways to improve a build, such as better enclosures, remote configuration and logging, and it lists further ideas like access point scanners, chat alerts and RF experiments. In audience questions, the speaker discussed when to use Bluetooth configuration instead of onboard buttons and screens, and which IDE suits MicroPython. The takeaway is to start small with a kit, experiment, and iterate on each device.

talks.title: So You Want to Give A Talk: How to Write a CFP
talks.teaser: Explains how to structure a conference call for papers, from titles and abstracts to outlines and bios.
talks.summary:
Phil Young opens by explaining why he built this session: first-time speakers often struggle to turn an idea into a conference submission, and the advice available online is plentiful but contradictory. Drawing on his years of reviewing submissions for BSides, DEF CON and Black Hat, he covers the reasons people choose to speak, from sharing research to enjoying the stage. He then describes the usual call-for-papers process, noting that most reviewers are volunteers, that submission windows typically open months ahead, and that a panel of several reviewers scores each proposal before track chairs rank them.

The middle of the talk walks through the parts of a submission. A title should be descriptive without being cryptic, and the abstract works as marketing that hints at the content without giving it away. The bio should be written in the third person and explain why this speaker is the right one for the topic. Young calls the outline the most important section, because reviewers use it to judge whether the speaker knows what they will cover, and the same outline can later become the structure of the slides. He also warns against using generative AI for the written sections, submitting one talk unchanged to many conferences, and co-presenting a first talk.

He closes with practical habits: keep a copy of every submission, spell check, ask peers to review drafts, and remember that a rejection often reflects heavy competition rather than poor quality. Listeners come away with a clearer picture of what a submission needs and what a first-time speaker can expect.

talks.title: When the Breach Hits the Fan: Understanding Cyber Insurance
talks.teaser: Breaks down what cyber insurance covers, how underwriting and claims work, and how businesses can partner with carriers.
talks.summary:
Mea Clift, who has spent decades in security leadership and now advises insurance underwriters, opens by placing cyber coverage alongside general liability and other business lines. She explains that general liability generally does not treat electronic data as tangible property, while cyber policies cover first-party costs such as forensics, data restoration, extortion response, and business interruption measured as lost income. Third-party coverage addresses claims arising from vendor breaches, privacy violations, and regulatory proceedings.

The talk then tackles common misconceptions, including a rumored exclusion for a specific endpoint security product, which she said is not how underwriting works. She covers the war exclusion, which is being reconsidered as conflict moves into cyber operations, and betterment coverage, which applies only after a covered event and typically does not replace whole systems. Fines are covered only under some policies and jurisdictions. Underwriters look at basics such as MFA, patching of actively exploited vulnerabilities, asset inventory, recovery speed, and vendor risk. Trends discussed include ransomware and business email compromise, along with claims tied to biometric privacy laws and tracking technologies.

Her practical advice is to report incidents early, since carriers can connect policyholders to breach response teams quickly, to answer questionnaires candidly with a security leader involved, to run business impact analyses that include managed service providers, and to treat the carrier relationship as an ongoing partnership. The session closed with audience questions about warning signs in policies and in customers.

talks.title: Dungeons & Dragons: The security tool you didn't know you needed
talks.teaser: Shows how role-playing game mechanics can make incident response tabletop exercises more engaging and memorable.
talks.summary:
The speakers start from a common problem: traditional tabletop exercises for incident response often feel scripted and dull. Participants protect their own turf, hold back in front of bosses or peers, or fight the scenario, so little is learned. They argue that engagement drives learning and that a fun format does not make training less serious. They separate game-based learning, where the game itself teaches, from gamification, where a competition is layered onto unrelated material, and point to research supporting collaborative play.

The core of the talk is a role-playing framework they call Hackback. An incident master runs the scenario much like a dungeon master, telling the story and adjusting difficulty so players neither fail nor succeed every time. Players take on characters such as a CFO, a marketing manager or an IT admin, each with modifiers and stereotyped traits that help people get into role. A d20 roll introduces randomness, so well-laid plans do not always work, which mirrors real incidents. The speakers ran a short demonstration of a Friday-afternoon alert about an administrator signing in from an unexpected country, showing how technical and communication choices get debated. They said the same structure can explain concepts such as zero trust, support risk assessments, and run red, purple or ransomware negotiation exercises.

To close, they described a malware-themed collectible game, an open-source plan with a private repository and a community Discord, and a workshop. In questions they said running a session well takes practice and security knowledge, and that teams can use their own runbooks. The main takeaway is that role-play can build empathy across roles and make response practice more realistic.

talks.title: Locking Hands: Ransomware Meets Bioimplants
talks.teaser: Shows how an educational ransomware locks NFC bioimplants, covering memory layout, password handling and a decryptor.
talks.summary:
Mauro Eldritch presented LockSkin, an educational ransomware experiment aimed at NFC bioimplants, the small subdermal chips some people inject into their hands to unlock doors, cars and devices. He noted that many owners skip a password or choose an easy one, which became the entry point for the work.

Reverse engineering was central: implant memory is tiny, and the password is stored as a short four-byte transform that each application computes with its own proprietary function, so only the originating tool can verify it. The team dumped and compared memory from encrypted and unencrypted tags, using an AI model to spot differences, and avoided permanent lock pages. Practical hurdles followed: limited reader range, a custom build inside a door knob with a PN532 reader and an ESP32, tight memory, and log retrieval over Wi-Fi. Several test tags were bricked.

The talk closed with a decryptor that sends raw NFC commands using the known password to reset the tag, showing the damage is reversible. Takeaways: treat implant passwords as a real control, know which memory regions are permanent before writing, and expect new interfaces to add attack surface.

talks.title: The Art of Concealment: CVE’s Challenge
talks.teaser: Examines gaps in CVE record quality, from missing weakness, product and patch data to a new CNA scorecard.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures program, which began in 1999 with a simple goal of giving each vulnerability a standard identifier and description. The speaker argues that the promise of a common, usable record has eroded as the number of organizations allowed to publish CVEs has grown past 460, each with its own conventions for what goes into a record.

The core of the argument is that a CVE record needs a few pieces to be useful to defenders: a weakness classification, an identifier for the affected product, a severity score, and a clear patch reference. Drawing on recent publishing data, the speaker notes that only a small share of new records carry a product identifier, while weakness and severity fields are far more common. Patch information is usually scattered among many references. The loss of NVD enrichment in 2024 exposed how much scanners and automation had depended on that data, and the schema validation for record descriptions is minimal.

To make these gaps measurable, the speaker introduced CNA Scorecard, an open source site that refreshes several times a day and counts which required fields each publishing organization fills in across recent records. The launch counts fields rather than judging content quality. The talk closes by asking vendors to treat complete vulnerability records as part of what customers pay for, and it points to upcoming EU publishing rules as a factor that could either raise or lower the bar.

talks.title: From Interview Questions to Cluster Damage: Adventures in k8s Cluster Shenanigans
talks.teaser: Explores Kubernetes cluster disruption scenarios, from DNS failure to malicious admission webhooks, and the defenses that counter them.
talks.summary:
The talk grew out of the questions the presenters ask job candidates in security interviews: a free-form game about how someone would disrupt or quietly misuse a working Kubernetes cluster. The speakers opened with a short primer on core objects such as pods, deployments, namespaces, service accounts and secrets. They pointed out that secrets are only base64 encoded and that namespaces are a weak boundary that depends entirely on role-based access control.

The middle of the session walked through several scenarios. Taking down CoreDNS breaks new name lookups across the cluster, yet image pulls still worked because the kubelet resolves names through the node's own resolver. Pinning CoreDNS to a node label and scaling its replica set to zero proved more stubborn than expected, since a leftover pod kept DNS alive until both were changed. A malicious validating admission webhook was then shown forwarding every new secret or pod definition to an external server. Finally, a monitoring tool's Prometheus endpoint exposed cluster-wide inventory in a single request, which is hard to spot in normal traffic.

The takeaways were practical: restrict who can change kube-system components and webhooks, alert on webhook configuration changes, use network policies to limit workload access, and verify that security products actually monitor what their vendors claim.

talks.title: UNION SELECT * FROM hackers: Why We Should Be Building InfoSec Worker Power Through the Labor Movement
talks.teaser: Makes the case that information security workers can build collective power through unions, and outlines practical steps to organize.
talks.summary:
Logan Arkema argues that information security workers have long relied on individual reputations and scarce skills for influence and job security, and that this approach is fragile as layoffs, AI-driven cost cutting and attacks on federal workforce protections mount. The talk opens by describing the current climate for security workers in government and the private sector, then contrasts it with the self-organizing habits the hacker community already has, from volunteer-run conferences to open source governance.

The middle section explains how unions work in the United States. Arkema walks through forming a union, bargaining a contract, and the concerted-activity rights that private-sector employees keep even without a union, and notes that federal workers face different limits. He points to examples from other tech workers, including Alphabet Workers Union actions at Google and a staff union at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, along with a nurses' union that is pursuing a ransomware clause in its contract. He also answers common objections, such as unions being ineffective, costly or hostile to high performers.

The closing segment argues that security staff hold real leverage because organizations depend on their systems, and urges listeners to build relationships, join groups such as the Tech Workers Coalition, and act collectively. Attendees leave with concrete starting points rather than a legal guide, along with a caveat that labor law varies and specialist advice is worth seeking before taking risky steps.

talks.title: When Attackers Tune In: Weaponizing LLM Tuning for Stealthy C2 and Exfiltration
talks.teaser: Shows how "what if" attacks on a Kubernetes cluster can disrupt DNS, exfiltrate secrets through webhooks, and enumerate services quietly.
talks.summary:
The talk is framed as a set of "what if" scenarios about how an attacker could disrupt or abuse a Kubernetes cluster, drawn from the open-ended questions the speakers ask job candidates. It opens with a primer on core objects such as pods, deployments, namespaces, service accounts, role bindings and secrets, and points out that a namespace is a soft security boundary that depends entirely on RBAC.

The middle section covers attacks. Patching the CoreDNS DaemonSet and scaling its replica set to zero breaks cluster name resolution, but the speakers note that the kubelet resolves image pulls through the node's own resolver, so some workloads keep running while others fail in cascading timeouts. A malicious validating admission webhook can quietly receive copies of new secrets, config maps and pods, and a live demo showed this with a small listening server. The speakers also show that a monitoring tool's exposed Prometheus-style API can reveal nodes, pods, containers, namespaces and load balancers in a single request that blends in with normal traffic.

For defenders, the takeaways are tighter RBAC, reviewing webhook configurations and alerting when they change, applying network policies around workloads, and checking whether a security product really sees both control-plane and runtime activity. The speakers stress that vendor visibility claims should be verified rather than trusted.

talks.title: Breaking the Illusion: Bypassing Endpoint Security Controls
talks.teaser: Shows how built-in tools and misconfigurations let attackers disable Zscaler and Microsoft Defender protections.
talks.summary:
The talk challenges marketing that calls endpoint products tamperproof. The presenters, both adversary emulation staff at PayPal, treat endpoint defenses as a full stack. That includes agents such as Microsoft Defender and supporting tools like the Zscaler client, plus management pushes through Intune or SCCM. Their starting point was prior CVEs for each product.

The demonstrations began with Zscaler. Its uninstall protection could be skipped with built-in PowerShell and WMI commands, and deleting a stored password from the keychain made the uninstaller fail open. Other methods blocked agent traffic with a Windows filtering tool, looped a task kill against the tunnel process, edited proxy rules, or renamed a blocked tool to an allowed name. For Defender, the speakers silenced cloud telemetry, restored quarantined tools through the local console, and disabled scanning by changing permissions on definition folders or replacing a key DLL. They also showed retrieval of BitLocker recovery keys as a low-privileged user, disabling Mark of the Web, and deactivating backup systems through a vendor console.

Many of these issues have since been patched or need configuration changes. Zscaler fixed 14 of 17 reported issues, while Microsoft closed its reports noting that admin access allows more damage. The takeaways: treat local admin as full compromise, monitor for tampering with agent files and services, check for persistence such as local admin password changes and immutable flags, and confirm that controls fail closed.
